tier_reason: bench-cross-results.md is the project's own snapshot from public code (tools/bench-cross.sh with bench/micros and bench/macros fixtures, Cynic built with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast) and states engine versions and the kernel, but no CPU model and no build flags for the jsvu-installed qjs binary, so it falls short of A; first-party, so C.

corrections.baseline: QuickJS-NG (qjs 0.15.1, prebuilt binary installed via jsvu per tools/bench-cross.sh, which names QuickJS-NG the headline non-JIT peer)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cynic revision 6e125807 built by tools/bench-cross.sh with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (Zig version pinned in build.zig.zon), run with --no-jit (macros also --unhardened); qjs is the jsvu-installed QuickJS-NG binary, build flags not stated
corrections.caveats: The results file calls itself an 'internal regression compass - not published', host-local and not comparable across hosts; CPU model missing, so tier C. Times are subprocess wall clock (spawn to exit), so process startup is included. The baseline is QuickJS-NG via jsvu, not Bellard's QuickJS; Cynic vendors QuickJS's libregexp. The comparison is interpreter tier only: on the same page Hermes, JavaScriptCore (JSC_useJIT=0) and V8 --jitless beat Cynic on every macro fixture, and in the full-speed table (JIT on) Cynic is about 4.5-12.6x slower than the fastest of V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore on every macro fixture (derived from page data; that table has no qjs row), with Cynic's JIT-on macro times barely different from its --no-jit times. Cynic is strict-only (no sloppy mode or Annex B), so it runs a narrower language than qjs. qjs uses far less memory: peak RSS 1.8 MB versus 6-12.5 MB for Cynic on all fixtures except splay. Micro fixtures are chosen by the author and 13 of 19 Cynic micro cells carry more than 10% spread (promise_chain 51%, prop_write 65%). README makes no comparative claim; the engine is pre-alpha.

notes: All claimed micro and macro numbers match the page exactly (18 of 18 completed micro fixtures faster than qjs, deltablue slower, richards a tie). Main shortcomings: baseline is QuickJS-NG via a jsvu binary, internal unpublished snapshot without CPU model, interpreter-tier only (Hermes, JSC and V8 jitless all faster on macros), and the JIT tier is 4.5-12.6x behind V8/SM/JSC.

tier_reason: The README chart (docs/Benchmark.png) shows 8.05 ms vs NLua 36.45 ms and MoonSharp 19.87 ms; the benchmark code is public (sandbox/Benchmark/AddBenchmark.cs with add.lua, BenchmarkDotNet 0.14.0, net8.0, MoonSharp 2.0.0, NLua 1.7.3) but CPU, runtime build and which variant (DoString or DoFile) the chart plots are not stated, so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet 0.14.0 ShortRun job with 10 warmup and 10 measured iterations and MemoryDiagnoser, target net8.0 (sandbox/Benchmark/Benchmark.csproj); baselines MoonSharp 2.0.0 and NLua 1.7.3 NuGet packages; build configuration and runtime used for the chart not stated
corrections.workload: add.lua loop calling a host C# add(x, 1) function 25,001 times (for _ = 0, 25000), timed through DoString/DoFile so script compilation is included; time and managed allocation per invocation (sandbox/Benchmark/AddBenchmark.cs).
corrections.caveats: The README shows only a chart image (docs/Benchmark.png) with no CPU, .NET runtime version or commit, and does not say whether the DoString or DoFile variant was plotted; the source is in sandbox/Benchmark/AddBenchmark.cs but not linked from the README. The workload measures host-call interop overhead (NLua marshals through reflection-registered methods into native Lua), not Lua execution speed, so it says nothing about Lua-CSharp's VM versus PUC Lua; the repo has an NBodyBenchmark with no published numbers. A .NET library, not callable from C++. First-party numbers.

notes: Chart numbers match the record exactly (about 4.5x vs NLua and 2.5x vs MoonSharp, derived from page data; 31.3 KB vs 12,306.5 KB and 13,887 KB allocated). Benchmark code exists in sandbox/Benchmark, correcting the record's claim that it is absent. Main shortcoming: interop-call microbenchmark only, no hardware, chart variant unstated.

tier_reason: The README table (2026-06-15) comes from the public bench-v8.sh (runs boa-dev's combined.js V8 suite once per engine) with release flags in Cargo.toml, but no CPU model, rustc version or qjs version/build is stated; first-party, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with the Cargo.toml release profile (opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units 1, panic = abort); rustc version not stated; qjs taken from PATH, version and build not stated
corrections.caveats: Headline 'outperforms QuickJS in benchmarks' contradicts the README's own overall score (1075 vs qjs 1101, -2.4%, slightly slower); the win is confined to RegExp (+174.8%) and NavierStokes (+18.6%). bench-v8.sh runs each engine once (one sample, no repeats) and picks whatever qjs is on PATH, so QuickJS version (Bellard or QuickJS-NG) is unknown; no CPU stated. RegExp passes only 42.3% of test262 RegExp tests (Promise 5.6%, Proxy 0%), which weakens the RegExp comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo; MIT is declared only in Cargo.toml and the README. A search snippet of an earlier announcement quoted 1256 vs 1219 (not on the page opened, so not used).

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; record already reports that pipa is slower than qjs overall. Main shortcomings: not faster overall (score -2.4%), single-run harness, unknown qjs build, low test262 conformance behind the RegExp win, no LICENSE file (MIT only in Cargo.toml/README).
